cover.description: A themed title page; optional subtitle, logo and metadata collapse when omitted.

running-head.description: Document title/section tracker and page fields, inherited by subsequent sections.

section-opener.description: A numbered section heading which sets the general section tracker.

key-takeaways.description: Executive conclusions with bounded one-line takeaways. Copy and adapt this document-local example.

source-line.description: A hairline and a source line in the source role, under a figure or a table. The data blocks invoke it; copy it to add a source to anything else.

kpi-row.description: Two to four headline metrics in equal columns: value with its unit, label, and a signed delta with a direction glyph; four of them set the figures a size smaller. An optional source collapses with its hairline. Text budgets reject overflow; columns reflow at unchanged type size.

unit.description: Suffix drawn after the figure at half its size: %, €m, pts. Write the space yourself when one belongs.

delta.description: Signed change shown beside the figure: +3.2 pts, −0.4.

trend.description: Direction glyph drawn before the delta.

figure-caption.description: The numbered caption under a figure: **Figure N.** and the text, N being a Word SEQ field over the figure sequence. chart-figure and figure invoke it, so charts and images number together.

chart-figure.description: A numbered, sourced chart: the chart itself (highcharts through the export server, or a native chart on the office-open renderer), a caption that says what it shows, an optional takeaway beneath, and the source line the report cites. The source is required; the figure number is a Word SEQ field.

chart.description: A highcharts or chart component. Put the unit in the value-axis title: Revenue (€m).

caption.description: What the chart shows, as a statement: Revenue by quarter, 2026.

takeaway.description: The one sentence the reader should leave with.

data-table.description: A sourced numeric table: a title, a text column of row labels at a fifth of the measure, one to five data columns right-aligned by construction, then optional notes and a source line. With its header, 24 rows keep the table on one page; the table-design rule checks the compiled table for mixed decimals.

labels.description: Row labels, top to bottom. Every data column lists its cells in this order and at this count.

header.description: Column header; put the unit here: Revenue (€m).

cells.description: One formatted value per row label, rounded the same way down the column.

numeric.description: Right-align header and cells so digits line up by place value. Set false for a text column.

notes.description: What the reader needs to interpret the figures: definitions, periods, exclusions.

callout.description: An aside set off by a hairline rule down its left edge: a short label over up to sixty words of text. No fill, so it reads as a note beside the argument rather than a box in it.

footnotes.description: Notes and sources: every distinct source-role slot value the document's block invocations carry, in order, as a numbered list under a label — the engine's /sources context. Emits nothing when no invocation cites a source.

metadata.title: Workforce Plan: Scaling from 240 to 400 Staff
metadata.author: Workforce Planning Team

slots.title: Workforce Plan: Scaling from 240 to 400 Staff
slots.subtitle: A Hiring, Retention and Mix-Shift Plan for the Managing Partners

slots.title: Hiring alone will not reach 400 staff

items: Growing from 240 to 400 staff needs roughly 280 hires against 17% attrition, rising to 26% in the three-to-five-year cohort.
Hiring at today's pace closes only 62% of the gap; the rest must come from retention and a shift toward junior hiring.
A targeted retention programme and mix-shift plan close the remaining gap for about £1.1m a year, roughly 5% of current payroll.

slots.source: Historic HR and finance data; workforce model, September 2026

props.text: Attrition already runs at 17% across the firm and rises to 26% among staff with three to five years' tenure — precisely the cohort the practice depends on to staff mid-sized engagements and to backfill outgoing partners. Recruiting at today's pace keeps pace with roughly six in ten of the hires the growth plan needs; the remainder has to come from keeping more of the people we already have, and from hiring a higher share of juniors who can be trained into the gap faster than laterals can be found. This plan sets out both moves together with the headcount bridge and the cost of delivering it.

slots.title: Attrition among mid-tenure staff drives the shortfall

props.text: Blended attrition of 17% masks a sharper problem inside the pyramid. Staff between their third and fifth year — the consultants and senior consultants who run engagements and mentor juniors — leave at 26% a year, roughly one-and-a-half times the firm average.

slots.caption: Attrition peaks at 26% among staff with three to five years' tenure
slots.takeaway: The three-to-five-year cohort leaves at one-and-a-half times the firm average, and it is this group the retention programme must target first.
slots.source: Internal HR system, tenure-banded attrition, FY2023–FY2026 average

props.text: This is the cohort the growth plan can least afford to lose. Replacing a departing senior consultant typically costs 50–150% of salary in recruitment, onboarding and lost productivity, and every unplanned departure in this band pushes a junior's promotion forward before they are ready, which risks pulling attrition higher still.

slots.title: The bridge to 400 needs 280 hires over three years

props.text: Reaching 400 staff by year three means adding a net 160 people on top of replacing everyone attrition takes. Under the recommended plan, retention actions bring blended attrition down from 17% toward 12.5% by year three, and hiring shifts toward junior grades to widen the pool the firm can draw on. The table below sets out the resulting headcount bridge.

slots.title: Recommended headcount bridge, current staff to 400 by year 3
slots.source: Workforce model, partners' workforce planning team, September 2026
slots.notes: Figures assume the recommended plan: retention actions cut blended attrition from a 17% baseline and hiring shifts toward junior grades. The year 3 closing headcount of 400 includes both external hires and internal promotions.

slots.label: Without the plan
slots.text: Hiring at today's pace alone — with attrition unchanged at 17% — reaches only about 341 staff by year three, roughly 59 short of the 400 target. The gap analysis below shows why relying on hiring alone is not enough.

slots.title: Retention and mix-shift close the gap for 5% more spend

props.text: Filling the remaining 38% of the gap needs three moves working together: a retention programme aimed squarely at the three-to-five-year cohort, faster internal promotion so senior roles are filled from within rather than through scarce lateral hires, and a shift in the hiring mix toward junior grades, where the market is deeper and time-to-hire is shorter.

items: Run a retention review for every consultant entering year three, with a compensation and career-path check before, not after, they consider leaving.
Introduce a retention bonus for the at-risk three-to-five-year cohort, vesting over 18 months, targeted at roughly 85 staff a year.
Add two senior recruiters and expand agency panels to lift sourcing capacity beyond the current 62% fill rate.
Shift the graduate and junior intake ratio from roughly 45% to 55% of new hires, backed by a structured 18-month development track.
Promote from within a year earlier where performance supports it, reducing reliance on scarce lateral senior hires.
Review workload and staffing on the highest-attrition accounts quarterly, and act on early-warning signals from exit interviews.

props.text: What the plan costs against the current run rate

Current payroll runs at approximately £20.4m a year for 240 staff, assuming a blended, fully loaded cost of about £85,000 per head. Reaching 400 staff under the recommended mix lifts the run rate to roughly £32m a year by year three — additional payroll expected to be funded by the fee income the extra headcount generates. The retention, recruiting and development plan itself needs about £1.05m a year on top of that, roughly 5% of today's run rate.

slots.title: Annual cost of the plan, against today's £20.4m payroll run rate
slots.notes: Figures are incremental to the current £20.4m payroll run rate (240 FTE at a blended £85k fully loaded cost) and exclude the payroll growth from adding headcount itself, which is expected to be revenue-funded.
slots.source: Finance business partner and workforce model, September 2026

slots.label: Payroll versus investment
slots.text: Growing to 400 staff lifts payroll itself from about £20.4m to about £32m a year — the direct, revenue-funded cost of growth. The £1.05m a year plan cost is separate: it secures the retention and hiring performance the growth depends on.
